title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene (613469) on chromosome 10q24.2.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that homozygous HPSE2 mutations cause UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping. We now report evidence that Heparanse 2 (HPSE2) is the culprit gene for the syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract places HPSE2 at 10q24. The finer band, 10q24.2, is standard gene-location nomenclature that restates this.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder marked by an abnormal facial expression and congenital obstructive uropathy (Wang et al., 1997; Wang et al., 1999). Affected individuals grimace when they try to smile, so that they appear to be crying when they smile (Derbent et al., 2009; Daly et al., 2010). The bladder fails to empty completely even though there is no anatomical outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage. Patients have enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction from neurogenic bladder (Wang et al., 1997). Reflux of infected urine to the upper renal tract puts the kidneys at risk of damage and renal failure (Daly et al., 2010). Some severely affected patients develop hypertension and progress to end-stage renal disease (Derbent et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families. One family was consanguineous, with parents who were first cousins. The patients had peculiar facies and gestures when smiling and crying. Their urinary findings included hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the prostatic and membranous urethra, and urethral valves. They also had an abnormal trabeculated bladder with diverticula and severe mucosal hypertrophy with sclerotic changes.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) carried out a genome screen that combined homozygosity mapping with DNA pooling. The study used 20 selected UFS patients, one patient pool, and 3 control pools of unaffected relatives. Of 36 random markers, D10S677 showed linkage and association with UFS. Patients had a significant excess of homozygosity at this marker compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)), and allele frequencies differed between patient and control pools. The authors then fine-mapped the gene with 10 additional markers spanning 22 cM, using haplotype (linkage disequilibrium) analysis. All 31 patients were homozygous for D10S1726 and D10S198, about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, compared with only 12% of unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-19)). Recombinations in patients who were heterozygous at the flanking markers D10S1433 and D10S603 placed the gene within a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Pang et al. (2010) found loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all of the urofacial syndrome patients they studied, who came from Colombia, the United States, and France. HPSE2 lies in the chromosome 10q24 region the authors had previously identified by homozygosity mapping.

checks.claim: Pang et al. (2010) found loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all urofacial syndrome patients they studied.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations with a loss of function in the Heparanase 2 (HPSE2) gene were identified in all UFS patients originating from Colombia, the United States, and France.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: The urofacial syndrome patients studied by Pang et al. (2010) came from Colombia, the United States, and France.
checks.evidence_quote: identified in all UFS patients originating from Colombia, the United States, and France
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: HPSE2 lies in the chromosome 10q24 region that Pang et al. (2010) had previously identified by homozygosity mapping.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping. We now report evidence that Heparanse 2 (HPSE2) is the culprit gene for the syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract identifies HPSE2 as the gene for the 10q24 region the authors had previously mapped, so the claim follows directly.

paragraphs.text: Within a 10q23-q24 autozygous region, Daly et al. (2010) found a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome. In 5 further unrelated families with the syndrome, they found homozygous HPSE2 mutations: exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations. They concluded that these findings confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) found a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene within a 10q23-q24 autozygous region in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24, within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) found homozygous HPSE2 mutations in 5 further unrelated families with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 mutations found by Daly et al. (2010) in 5 further urofacial syndrome families included exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) concluded that their findings confirmed HPSE2 as the gene causing urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Pang et al. (2010) noted that UFS patients completely lack HPSE2 function. On that basis, they suggested that HPSE2 may be important for coordinating the muscles used in facial expression and urine voiding.

checks.claim: Pang et al. (2010) noted that UFS patients completely lack HPSE2 function.
checks.evidence_quote: Complete loss of HPSE2 function in UFS patients suggests
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Pang et al. (2010) suggested that HPSE2 may be important for coordinating the muscles used in facial expression and urine voiding.
checks.evidence_quote: HPSE2 may be important for the synergic action of muscles implicated in facial expression and urine voiding.
checks.explanation: 'Synergic action of muscles' is fairly paraphrased as 'coordinating the muscles'.

paragraphs.text: Daly et al. (2010) showed that HPSE2 is expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system, where they suggested it might help control facial expression and urinary voiding. HPSE2 is also expressed in bladder smooth muscle, which the authors considered consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) showed that HPSE2 is expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system.
checks.evidence_quote: We show that HPSE2 is expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) suggested that HPSE2 in the central nervous system might help control facial expression and urinary voiding.
checks.evidence_quote: where it might be implicated in controlling facial expression and urinary voiding
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) showed that HPSE2 is expressed in bladder smooth muscle.
checks.evidence_quote: and also in bladder smooth muscle, consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) considered HPSE2 expression in bladder smooth muscle consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function.
checks.evidence_quote: and also in bladder smooth muscle, consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows the condition to be recognized early, which could help with early assessment and treatment and perhaps improve prognosis. Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) stated that the clear link between distorted facial expression and neuropathic bladder, which damages the genitourinary tract, should prompt urologic evaluation of anyone with 'inversion' of facial expression.

checks.claim: Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies of Ochoa syndrome allows early recognition of the condition.
checks.evidence_quote: The peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Elejalde (1979) noted that early recognition of Ochoa syndrome could help with early assessment and treatment and perhaps improve prognosis.
checks.evidence_quote: this can be helpful for early assessment and treatment, leading perhaps to a better prognosis.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) stated that there is a clear link between distorted facial expression and neuropathic bladder, which damages the genitourinary tract.
checks.evidence_quote: The clear association of distortion in facial expression and neuropathic bladder with resultant damage to the genitourinary tract
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.claim: Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) stated that anyone with 'inversion' of facial expression should undergo urologic evaluation.
checks.evidence_quote: should prompt urological evaluation of individuals with "inversion" of facial expression.
checks.explanation: The paper says the association 'should prompt' urological evaluation of such individuals. That is a recommendation to evaluate them, not a statement that everyone must undergo evaluation, so the claim slightly overstates it.

paragraphs.text: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001), Derbent et al. (2009), and Aydogdu et al. (2010) each stressed that early diagnosis, helped by recognizing the characteristic facial grimacing, is important for managing the urinary problems. Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) added that early diagnosis also matters for prognosis.

checks.claim: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001), Derbent et al. (2009), and Aydogdu et al. (2010) each stressed that early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome is important for managing the urinary problems.
checks.evidence_quote: Establishing an early diagnosis has important consequences for the management and prognosis of urinary problems in these patients.
checks.explanation: This paper supports its part of the claim. The other cited papers were not checked here.

checks.claim: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001), Derbent et al. (2009), and Aydogdu et al. (2010) each indicated that recognizing the characteristic facial grimacing helps early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: It is likely that they may be missed because of variability of the urinary problems and failure to recognize the characteristic facial grimacing.
checks.explanation: The paper says cases are missed when the grimacing goes unrecognized. That only implies recognizing it helps early diagnosis; the abstract does not say so outright. The other cited papers were not checked here.

checks.claim: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) stated that early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome also matters for prognosis.
checks.evidence_quote: Establishing an early diagnosis has important consequences for the management and prognosis of urinary problems in these patients.
checks.explanation: The abstract states that prognosis is affected.

paragraphs.text: Daly et al. (2010) used whole-genome SNP mapping in an individual with urofacial syndrome to define a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24. Within this region they found a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) used whole-genome SNP mapping in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Whole-genome SNP mapping in an individual with urofacial syndrome defined a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Within the 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24, a 10-kb deletion was found in the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The 10-kb HPSE2 deletion found in an individual with urofacial syndrome encompasses exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified
checks.explanation: Stated directly.
